raw_case_text:
A 52-year-old female, without any significant medical history, presented to our dermatology department (Skin Diseases and Leishmaniasis Research Center) with a 6-month history of an ulcerative cutaneous nodule on the posterior side of the right forearm. According to the patient, the lesion had initially appeared as a single painless and non-itchy papule and gradually progressed to a large crusted ulcerative nodule with an erythematous border [Figure 1a]. The patient had been treated with systemic antibiotics and local wound care for several months before referring to our department, although no improvement had been observed. The physical examination of the patient was unremarkable, and no systemic symptom such as fatigue, weakness, fever, night sweats, and weight loss was detected.
The skin lesion was initially suspected of being cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) because of its endemism in our country. However, the microscopic examination of the Giemsa-stained smears of skin lesion was negative. Therefore, the patient underwent an incisional biopsy of the skin lesion. The histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen showed a dense, diffuse, and monomorphous infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis, which rejected the diagnosis of CL. The infiltrate was composed of small lymphocytes with rounded hyper-chromatic nuclei without any atypical features, indicating a lymphoproliferative disorder [Figure 2]. The result of immuno-histochemistry analysis of skin lesion biopsy was positive for CD5, CD20, and BCL2 but negative for CD3, BCL6, cyclin-D1, and C10, suggesting a small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) [Figure 3]. Laboratory tests showed an elevated white blood cell (35.4 x 103/muL, normal range: 4-11 x 103/mu) and lymphocyte count (28320 lymphocytes/mcl, normal range: 800-500 lymphocytes/mcl), although the level of red blood cells (4.14 million/mm3, normal range: 4-5.4 million/mm3) and platelets (150 *1000/muL, normal range: 450 *1000/muL) were within the normal range. Microscopic examination of peripheral blood smears revealed the presence of numerous small lymphocytes with round nuclei, clumped chromatin and scant cytoplasm, few smudge cells, and 15% of prolymphocytes. Therefore, the patient was referred to an oncologist for a definitive diagnosis of the disease and treatment. Microscopic assessment of bone marrow biopsy indicated the proliferation of mature lymphocytes in interstitial and diffuse patterns. Flow cytometric analysis of bone marrow aspirate revealed mature lymphocytes expressing CD5+CD19, CD5, CD19, and CD23. The computed tomography (CT) scanning of the abdomen and pelvis was normal and excluded the involvement of the internal organs. Finally, the lesion was diagnosed as leukemia cutis (involving stage I of SLL/CLL). The patient underwent four cycles of systemic chemotherapy using rituximab, followed by one cycle of therapy with chlorambucil (2 mg/day). She tolerated the chemotherapy regimen very well. After 4 months of the treatment initiation, the lesion resolved completely [Figure 1b] and counts were in the normal range. Upon her last follow-up, which was 9 months after chemotherapy treatment, the patient was in complete remission and no sign of lesion recurrence was observed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old female presented with a 6-month history of a progressively enlarging ulcerative cutaneous nodule on the posterior right forearm.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The lesion began 6 months prior as a single painless, non-pruritic papule on the posterior right forearm and gradually enlarged into a crusted ulcerative nodule with an erythematous border. Several months of systemic antibiotics and local wound care prior to referral yielded no improvement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; resident of a cutaneous leishmaniasis-endemic region in Iran.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for local pain, pruritus, fatigue, weakness, fever, night sweats, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Large crusted ulcerative nodule with an erythematous border on the posterior aspect of the right forearm; systemic physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed leukocytosis (WBC 35.4 x 10^3/uL; ref 4-11 x 10^3/uL) and marked lymphocytosis (28,320 lymphocytes/uL; ref 800-5000/uL), with normal RBC count (4.14 million/mm3; ref 4-5.4 million/mm3) and platelets (150 x 10^3/uL). Peripheral blood smear showed numerous small mature lymphocytes with clumped chromatin and scant cytoplasm, smudge cells, and 15% prolymphocytes.
objective.advanced_workup: Giemsa-stained slit-skin smears of the forearm lesion were negative for Leishmania bodies. Incisional skin biopsy showed a dense, diffuse monomorphous dermal infiltrate of small lymphocytes positive for CD5, CD20, and BCL2 and negative for CD3, BCL6, cyclin-D1, and CD10. Bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry demonstrated interstitial and diffuse proliferation of mature lymphocytes expressing CD5+CD19+, CD5, CD19, and CD23; abdominal and pelvic CT was normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cutaneous leishmaniasis was ruled out by negative Giemsa skin smears and histopathology, and definitive immunophenotyping of the skin biopsy and bone marrow established B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL, stage I) presenting as leukemia cutis. Treatment with 4 cycles of systemic rituximab followed by 1 cycle of oral chlorambucil (2 mg/day) achieved complete resolution of the cutaneous lesion and normalization of blood counts within 4 months, with sustained complete remission at 9-month follow-up.
